item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q020_syntaxin_fragment_reclassification","answer":"In SCOPe 2.08, d1br0a_ and d1ez3a_/d1ez3b_/d1ez3c_ should no longer be interpreted as independent examples establishing a spectrin-like fold. SCOPe explicitly marks each as a “three-helical fragment; similar to one spectrin repeat” and with the ms caveat: secondary structures comprising less than one-third of the common domain are missing. They are placed with full syntaxin d1dn1b_ in class a (all-alpha), fold a.47 (STAT-like), superfamily a.47.2 (t-SNARE proteins), and family a.47.2.1 (t-SNARE proteins). Thus the full-domain evidence changes the biological reading from a fragment-defined structural resemblance to an incomplete instance of the syntaxin/t-SNARE domain architecture. Shared family and superfamily provide substantially stronger evolutionary support than shared fold alone; resemblance of the three-helix fragment to a spectrin repeat does not establish spectrin homology or justify transferring spectrin function. Likewise, a fragment should not determine whole-domain boundaries, missing-helix geometry, or function in an unrelated target. For classification or modeling, require full-length sequence/domain-boundary evidence plus alignment to a complete-domain structure, and prefer a complete current template such as 3c98 chain B: 1dn1 is obsolete in favor of 3c98, and SCOPe retains d1dn1b_ as an automated match to d3c98b_.
